passage:
I'm Vasudha, and I was hanging washing on the terrace when I saw my neighbour's daughter Elizabeth lying flat on her roof with a blanket, staring up. It was a clear night after the power cut, with stars everywhere. She didn't move for a long while.
When I whispered across and asked what she was doing, she said, "Just looking." Then, "It's so big, Aunty. It makes me feel tiny, but in a nice way." She was smiling.
Earlier that evening she had fretted loudly about a spelling test, and now she never mentioned it. I can't say exactly what she was thinking. I left her the quiet and went in.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth lie on the roof with?
qa.a: Elizabeth was lying flat on her roof with a blanket.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth feel as she looks at the stars?
qa.a: Tiny but happy. She says the sky is so big it makes her feel small in a nice way, and she is smiling.

qa.q: What did Vasudha choose to do when she saw Elizabeth?
qa.a: Vasudha whispered one question, listened, and then left Elizabeth alone with the sky instead of talking more.

qa.q: How does Vasudha see Elizabeth's stargazing?
qa.a: Vasudha notices the smile and that the spelling test worry has vanished, but admits she cannot say exactly what Elizabeth is thinking.

grounding: A child under a night sky feels small yet happy, and awe softens her earlier worry, seen by a neighbour.

passage:
Saturday. On the ferry across the wide river, Mohit stopped chattering. The far bank was a thin line and the water went on and on. His mother Salma asked if he was cold. "No," he said, holding the rail. "It's just so big."
Monday. At school he tried to tell a friend and got stuck for words. He drew the river across a whole page and left the boat as a tiny dot.
The next Saturday. Back on the ferry, Mohit stood quietly again. This time he grinned at Salma and said, "I feel small, but happy small." He did not ask for her phone once.

qa.q: What did Mohit draw at school on Monday?
qa.a: He drew the river across a whole page, with the boat as a tiny dot.

qa.q: What is Mohit feeling on the ferry, and how does he describe it the next Saturday?
qa.a: He is awed and quiet at first, then says he feels small but happy small.

qa.q: What did Mohit choose to do at school to share his awe?
qa.a: He drew the river across a whole page with a tiny boat when words failed him.

qa.q: What might Salma notice about Mohit between the two Saturdays?
qa.a: She may notice he is calmer and more thoughtful, since he stays quiet at the rail and does not ask for her phone.

grounding: A child looking at a huge river feels small yet happy, and awe expands his sense of the world.

passage:
Note from Vishal, physics teacher. After the visiting scientist's talk on how galaxies form, Payal stayed in her seat after the bell, eyes on the empty stage. She is usually first out for lunch. When I asked if all was well, she said, "Sir, the scientist said half of it is still unknown and she has spent forty years on it. I want to be like that."
She copied a line from the board into her diary and left without her tiffin. Later I saw her asking the librarian for the astronomy shelf. I will pass her name to the science club and offer her a book. No concern about Payal today: she seemed lifted, not upset.

qa.q: What did Payal leave behind when she walked out?
qa.a: Her tiffin.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling after the talk?
qa.a: She was inspired and lifted. She stayed in her seat, wanted to be like the scientist, and forgot her lunch.

qa.q: What could Vishal do next to support Payal's interest?
qa.a: Vishal plans to pass her name to the science club and offer her a book, giving her a route to follow her curiosity.

qa.q: How might the scientist's admission of not knowing half of it have affected Payal?
qa.a: It seems to have impressed Payal, since she wants to be like someone who keeps working on what is unknown.

grounding: A teenager moved by a scientist feels lifted beyond daily worries.

passage:
Thursday night. I left my bag in an auto this morning with my exam hall ticket in it. I nearly cried at the school gate. At lunchtime the guard called me out: the driver, Samir Bhai, had come all the way back, and he put the bag in my hands. I tried to give him money. He folded my fingers over it and said, "Beta, study well. That's my payment." Then he was gone before I could thank him properly.
I've been thinking about it all evening. My worries about tomorrow's paper feel smaller, like somebody opened a window. I want to be a person who does that for someone one day.
Leela

qa.q: What did Leela leave in the auto?
qa.a: A bag with the exam hall ticket in it.

qa.q: What is Leela feeling as Leela writes about Samir Bhai?
qa.a: Moved and lifted. Leela's exam worries feel smaller, like somebody opened a window, and Leela wants to be like Samir Bhai.

qa.q: What did Leela decide after Samir Bhai's kindness?
qa.a: Leela decided to become a person who does something like that for someone else one day.

qa.q: What might Samir Bhai have been thinking when he refused the money?
qa.a: He seems to have wanted nothing in return, only for Leela to study well, which is why he folded Leela's fingers over the money and left.

grounding: A teenager moved by a stranger's kindness feels lifted beyond daily worries.

passage:
Minakshi had two days off and a thin wallet, so she skipped the packaged trek and took the night bus to the hill temple with Lokesh. They started up the steps at four in the dark, torches bobbing, breath white. The climb was steeper than she had bargained for.
At the top, wrapped in one shared blanket, they watched the sky turn from black to grey to gold. Chanting floated up from the valley. All week she had stewed over a missed target at work, and now it looked like a small stone in a very large field.
On the way down she said, "That's the cheapest thing I've bought that actually worked."

qa.q: How did Minakshi travel to the hill temple?
qa.a: By night bus.

qa.q: How does Minakshi feel at the top of the hill?
qa.a: Awed and lighter. Her worry about the missed target shrinks to a small stone in a very large field.

qa.q: What choice did Minakshi make because money was short?
qa.a: She skipped the packaged trek and took the cheap night bus, showing that awe does not need a big budget.

qa.q: How might Lokesh feel sharing the blanket at sunrise?
qa.a: Probably as moved as Minakshi, since they watch the sky change together in silence.

grounding: A young adult makes time and a budget for a hill-temple sunrise, and the awe reduces petty stress.

passage:
Tejas had booked the observatory night three weeks earlier and put it in his calendar like a meeting. On Saturday he took a bus across Bengaluru with his friend Payal. On the rooftop they queued for a small telescope.
When his turn came he looked at Saturn: a tiny gold ring, sharp as a coin. "That's real?" he whispered. Payal nodded and said nothing.
The office inbox, the rent, the thing his manager said on Friday, all shrank away. On the bus home he said, "I want to do this every month."
"Put it in the calendar," said Payal.

qa.q: What did Tejas see through the telescope?
qa.a: Saturn: a tiny gold ring, sharp as a coin.

qa.q: What is Tejas feeling when he looks at Saturn?
qa.a: Wonder and quiet amazement. He whispers 'That's real?' and his office worries shrink away.

qa.q: What choice did Tejas make that made the night possible?
qa.a: He booked the observatory night three weeks early and put it in his calendar like a meeting.

qa.q: How does Payal respond to Tejas's wonder?
qa.a: Payal nods and says nothing, leaving space for the awe, and later suggests putting the next one in the calendar.

grounding: A young adult makes time for an observatory night, and the awe reminds him that problems are part of something larger.

passage:
Trisha: You went so quiet at the viewpoint
Trisha: I almost asked if you were okay
Bhupen: I was fine. Just the whole valley
Trisha: I could tell. So I stood there and said nothing 😅
Bhupen: Honestly the best part of the day. Thank you for not filling it
Trisha: I wanted to say "wow" like ten times

Trisha: Deal

qa.a: At the viewpoint.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling at the viewpoint, and what did Trisha do about it?
qa.a: Trisha was tempted to speak, wanting to say 'wow' ten times, but chose to stand quietly.

qa.q: What choice by Trisha does Bhupen thank Trisha for?
qa.a: Trisha did not fill the silence and just stood there beside Bhupen.

qa.q: What was it like for Bhupen at the viewpoint?
qa.a: Bhupen was absorbed by the whole valley. The silence felt like the best part of the day.

passage:
Deepika had walked Aditi up the old fort hill at dawn, out of town and past the buffalo sheds. At the top the plains opened below them, silver with river mist, and Aditi stopped mid-sentence and stayed stopped. Her hands fell open at her sides.
Deepika had a joke ready and a question about breakfast. She swallowed both. She watched the light climb Aditi's face and said not a word for a long time.
When a farmer's cough floated up from below, Aditi sighed and said, "Thank you for not talking."
"I wanted to," Deepika admitted.
"I know," said Aditi, laughing. "That's why it counts."

qa.q: Where did Deepika and Aditi go at dawn?
qa.a: Up the old fort hill.

qa.q: What is Deepika feeling as she stays silent at the top?
qa.a: She is tempted to joke and ask about breakfast, but she holds back and lets the moment breathe.

qa.q: What choice did Deepika make that Aditi valued?
qa.a: She swallowed her joke and her question and stayed silent, letting Aditi's awe breathe.

qa.q: How does Aditi feel about Deepika's silence?
qa.a: Grateful. She thanks Deepika, and says it counts because Deepika wanted to speak and did not.

grounding: A person standing with a friend before a great view sees the friend go quiet and does not fill the silence.

passage:
Kashish burst into tears when the fireworks banged outside the flat, and ran to Mummy. Jaya lifted her onto her lap on the sofa and wrapped both arms round her. She did not say much, just rocked slowly and hummed.
Kashish's sobs became hiccups, then long slow breaths, in and out. Her fingers loosened from Jaya's kurta. She rested her head on Jaya's shoulder and stared at the fan, quite still.
Later she whispered, "Your chest is warm." She stayed there until Papa called dinner, and even then she took her time.

qa.q: What frightened Kashish?
qa.a: The fireworks banging outside the flat.

qa.q: What is Kashish feeling as she rests in Jaya's lap?
qa.a: Safe and calm. Her sobs turn to slow breaths, her fingers loosen and she says Jaya's chest is warm.

qa.q: What did Jaya do that helped Kashish settle?
qa.a: Jaya held her close, rocked slowly and hummed, saying little, so her calm could be borrowed.

qa.q: How might Jaya feel as Kashish's breathing slows?
qa.a: Probably relieved and tender, since she stays holding Kashish quietly and does not hurry her.

grounding: A child rests in a parent's lap and breathes slowly, storing calm as a felt memory of safety.

passage:
Thunder rolled over the flat.
Rafiq: Amma, the sky is shouting.
Yamini: It is loud tonight. Come here.
Rafiq: Will it stop?
Yamini: It always does. Sit on my lap. Can you feel my heartbeat?
Rafiq: Thump, thump.
Yamini: Slow and steady. Copy it.
Rafiq: ...In. Out.
Yamini: That's it.
Rafiq: Amma? The sky is quieter now.
Yamini: Or you are. Shall I hum?
Rafiq: Yes. Don't go.

qa.q: What did Rafiq say the sky was doing?
qa.a: Shouting.

qa.q: What is Rafiq feeling when the thunder rolls, and how does it change?
qa.a: Rafiq is scared at first and wants to be held, then feels calmer breathing with Yamini's slow heartbeat, though Rafiq still asks Yamini to stay.

qa.q: What did Yamini do to help Rafiq feel calm?
qa.a: Yamini invited Rafiq onto her lap, let Rafiq feel the steady heartbeat and asked Rafiq to copy it.

qa.q: What might Yamini be thinking when she says 'Or you are'?
qa.a: She notices that Rafiq has become calmer and gently points it out to Rafiq.

grounding: A child rests on a parent's lap during a storm and borrows calm from the adult's slow heartbeat.

passage:
Sunday. In the quiet before dinner, Jyoti taught her son Rafiq a game: smell the flower, blow out the candle. They did it five times, giggling. She also showed him where the water jug stood.
Wednesday. Rafiq lost at carrom, flung the striker and stomped off. Jyoti did not chase him or say "calm down." She waited.
Saturday. Rafiq lost again. His face went red. Then he walked to the jug, drank a glass of water, stepped onto the balcony and took five slow breaths. When he came back he said, "I'm still annoyed, but I'm okay. Rematch?"

qa.q: What game did Jyoti teach Rafiq on Sunday?
qa.a: Smell the flower, blow out the candle.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling when he flung the striker on Wednesday?
qa.a: Angry and frustrated at losing the carrom game, which is why he stomped off.

qa.q: What did Jyoti choose not to do on Wednesday, and why might that matter?
qa.a: She did not chase him or tell him to calm down. The skill had been taught on a calm Sunday, so she trusted him to use it.

qa.q: How might Jyoti feel watching Rafiq on Saturday?
qa.a: Probably proud and relieved, since Rafiq drinks water, steps out and breathes without being told.

grounding: A child practises slowing breathing and drinking water while calm, then uses it after being upset.

passage:
Wasim, come and sit with your Dada Suraj. When I was your age I had a temper like a firecracker. One day at the tea stall I threw my slate because I couldn't do a sum. My mother didn't shout. That evening, when I was calm, she showed me: "When the anger comes, drink water slowly and step outside for a minute."
I laughed. But the next time I lost a game of marbles, I remembered. I drank from the earthen pot, walked to the neem tree and counted my breaths. The anger drained away like water through sand.
She never told me in the moment I was furious. Only before. That's why it worked.

qa.q: What did Suraj throw at the tea stall?
qa.a: His slate.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel when he lost the game of marbles?
qa.a: Angry, like a firecracker, but he remembered his mother's words and let the anger drain away.

qa.q: What choice did young Suraj make when he lost at marbles?
qa.a: He drank water from the earthen pot, walked to the neem tree and counted his breaths.

qa.q: Why did Suraj's mother speak to him in the evening and not in the moment?
qa.a: She waited until he was calm, when he could listen, so the skill was ready before the next storm.

grounding: An elder recalls learning to drink water and step outside when angry, taught before the storm.

passage:
When the science-fair model collapsed an hour before judging, Hemant's heart hammered. Two classmates were shouting at each other and someone was close to tears. Devika just looked at the pieces, took a breath and said, "Okay. What do we still have?" Her voice was flat.
"She doesn't even care," Hemant muttered to another boy.
Then he noticed her hands sorting screws into a lid, and that she had tied her hair back before anyone spoke. She wasn't indifferent. She was steady. By judging time the model stood, slightly crooked.
Hemant felt ashamed. "Sorry," he told her. "I thought you didn't care."
"I saw all of it," said Devika. "I just didn't want to add to it."

qa.q: What happened an hour before judging?
qa.a: The science-fair model collapsed.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel afterwards about what he said?
qa.a: Ashamed. He realised Devika had been steady, not uncaring, and apologised.

qa.q: What could Hemant do differently the next time a classmate stays composed in a crisis?
qa.a: He could watch what the person does, such as sorting screws and tying back hair, before deciding they don't care, and ask instead of assuming.

qa.q: How does Devika see her own calm?
qa.a: She sees it as a choice not to add to the panic. She noticed all of it but did not want to make it worse.

grounding: Peers see a composed teenager and assume indifference, but the calm is a steady response to a problem she fully sees.

passage:
Jagdish: You didn't even flinch when the coach shouted. Do you care about the team at all?
Ankita: I did care. I heard every word.
Jagdish: You looked bored.
Ankita: I was thinking about what he said, and which part was fair.
Jagdish: I'd have been fuming.
Ankita: I was upset. Inside. But if I'd shouted back, we'd lose the next match too.
Jagdish: Hm. I thought calm meant you didn't mind.
Ankita: It's the opposite. I mind, so I'm not throwing my bag.
Jagdish: Fair. Sorry.
Ankita: Come to practice early? We can fix the passing drill.

qa.q: What did Jagdish accuse Ankita of on the bus stop?
qa.a: Not caring about the team.

qa.q: What did Jagdish believe Ankita's calm meant?
qa.a: Jagdish believed calm meant Ankita did not mind, until Ankita explained about being upset inside.

qa.q: What could Jagdish and Ankita do next, according to Ankita?
qa.a: Come to practice early and fix the passing drill together.

qa.q: How does Ankita feel about the coach's shouting?
qa.a: Upset inside, but Ankita chooses not to shout back, because it could cost the next match too.

grounding: Peers see a composed teenager and assume indifference, but real calm notices the problem and chooses not to be thrown.

passage:
The interview for the internship was running an hour late, the waiting room was packed, and the ceiling fan had stopped. Usha was pacing and muttering about how many candidates there were.
Bhavna felt her pulse in her ears and her palms were damp. She noticed it the way you notice a bird on a wire, and told herself: the nerves are here, the panel isn't mine to control, my answers are. She folded her hands, breathed out slowly, and rehearsed only her first line.
"Aren't you scared?" whispered Usha.
"Yes," said Bhavna. "I'm just not leaving."
When her name was called she stood up, shaky and steady at once.

qa.q: Why was the waiting room uncomfortable?
qa.a: The interview was running an hour late, the room was packed and the ceiling fan had stopped.

qa.q: What is Bhavna feeling as she waits, and how does she handle it?
qa.a: Bhavna is nervous, with a pounding pulse and damp palms, but she accepts the nerves and focuses on what she can control.

qa.q: What choice did Bhavna make that kept her steady?
qa.a: She separated what was not hers to control from her answers, breathed slowly and rehearsed only her first line.

qa.q: How might Usha be feeling in the waiting room?
qa.a: Anxious and restless, since Usha paces and mutters about how many candidates there are.

grounding: A student before an interview feels nerves but stays steady, having accepted that not everything is in her control.

passage:
Vikas sat outside the department seminar room in Delhi, gripping a glass of water he wasn't drinking. His viva began in ten minutes. His knees bounced and his stomach felt like a knot.
Farida, his lab-mate, sat beside him and did not tell him to relax. He said, "I might forget everything."
"You might," she said. "Then you say, 'Let me think,' and the world doesn't end."
He nodded. He couldn't control the examiners' moods, the questions or the clock. He could control his first sentence. When the door opened he stood. His voice shook on the first line, and by the third answer it was his own.

qa.q: How long until Vikas's viva began?
qa.a: In ten minutes.

qa.q: What is Vikas feeling outside the seminar room?
qa.a: Nervous and afraid of forgetting everything, shown by his bouncing knees and the knot in his stomach.

qa.q: What did Vikas decide to focus on?
qa.a: His first sentence, since he cannot control the examiners' moods, the questions or the clock.

qa.q: How does Farida try to help Vikas?
qa.a: Farida does not tell him to relax. She admits he might forget and gives him a phrase to use, 'Let me think', which makes forgetting survivable.

grounding: A student before a viva feels nerves yet stays steady, having accepted that not everything is in his control.

passage:
Ganga: Kamal are you there? I think I'm going to fail tomorrow
Kamal: I'm here. What's happening?
Ganga: The presentation. My hands are shaking and I can't even open the slides
Kamal: ok. I'm not going anywhere. Put me on speaker and tell me slide one
Ganga: ...fine. It's the title. That's all I know
Kamal: Good, that's one slide. What's slide two?
Ganga: Data. I do know the data
Kamal: See? You know more than the panic says. Drink some water, I'll stay on
Ganga: ok. My heart's slowing a bit. Thanks for not panicking with me 🙂
Kamal: Anytime. Sleep after slide five 😴

qa.q: What is slide one of Ganga's presentation?
qa.a: The title.

qa.q: What is Ganga feeling at the start of the chat?
qa.a: Ganga is panicked and afraid of failing, with shaking hands and unable to open the slides.

qa.q: What small step helped Ganga calm down?
qa.a: Kamal stayed on the line, asked for one slide at a time and suggested drinking water, so Ganga could see how much was known.

qa.q: How does Kamal seem to see Ganga's panic?
qa.a: Kamal treats it as something that says less than Ganga knows, stays calm and lets Ganga's own knowledge answer the fear.

grounding: A worried person's panic eases near a calm friend, and being that steadiness is a gift.

passage:
The monsoon had washed out the road, and the wedding cars were two hours late. Zeenat paced the courtyard gripping her dupatta, her breath quick and high. "What if the muhurat passes? What if they never come?"
Ira Masi, in her plastic chair, was shelling peas. "Sit here, beta," she said. "Drink."
Zeenat sat, sipped, and watched Ira's slow, steady fingers.
"I've called the driver," said Ira. "The road is open on the far side and they are coming round. We can't move the river, but we can lay out the plates."
Zeenat's breathing slowed to the rhythm of the peas. By the time the horn sounded at the gate, she was laying out plates beside Ira.

qa.q: What had the monsoon washed out?
qa.a: The road.

qa.q: What is Zeenat feeling in the courtyard?
qa.a: Panicked and afraid the muhurat will pass, shown by her pacing, her quick high breath and her grip on her dupatta.

qa.q: What did Ira do that steadied Zeenat?
qa.a: Ira kept shelling peas, offered a seat and water, said she had called the driver and gave Zeenat a task, laying out plates.

qa.q: How might Ira see the situation compared with Zeenat?
qa.a: Ira seems to accept what cannot be changed, like the river, and focuses on what can be done, so she stays calm.

grounding: A worried person feels panic ease near a calm elder, and calm spreads between people.

passage:
The bus stand was loud and crowded, a horn blaring every few seconds, and Nandini was tired. When the conductor handed over her ticket, her mother Rehana nudged her. "What do we say?"
"Thank you," said Nandini flatly, looking at her shoes.
Rehana did not scold. At the next stop the fruit seller passed a banana up through the window, and Rehana said warmly, "Thank you, that looks so sweet," looking straight at him. Nandini watched.
At the third stop she said it to the seller herself, with no nudge. "Thank you." This time she looked up.

qa.q: Who nudged Nandini to say thank you?
qa.a: Her mother Rehana.

qa.q: How does Nandini feel when she says 'Thank you' to the conductor?
qa.a: Tired and just going through the motions. She says it flatly and looks at her shoes.

qa.q: What choice did Rehana make instead of scolding?
qa.a: She modelled a warm thank you to the fruit seller, looking at him, so Nandini could watch how it is done.

qa.q: What might the fruit seller feel when Nandini says thank you and looks up?
qa.a: Probably pleased and noticed, since the thanks comes with eye contact.

grounding: A child says thank you because she was told to, and repetition and modelling plant the habit before the feeling.

passage:
Every morning Siddharth chirped "Thank you, bhaiya!" to the watchman without breaking stride. It came out like part of the alphabet. His mother Lakshmi noticed he never looked up.
One rainy day she slowed at the gate. "Thank you for holding the umbrella for us, bhaiya. You got wet," she said, and smiled at him. The watchman smiled back and his shoulders eased.
Siddharth stopped skipping. The next morning he said the same words, then glanced up. The watchman waved.
It wasn't feeling yet, just a small peek. Lakshmi went on saying hers aloud.

qa.q: What did Siddharth say to the watchman every morning?
qa.a: 'Thank you, bhaiya!'

qa.q: What does Lakshmi seem to worry about in Siddharth's thank-yous?
qa.a: That they are only a rote phrase with no feeling yet, since he says it like part of the alphabet and never looks up.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi do to show Siddharth a different way of saying thanks?
qa.a: She slowed at the gate, named what the watchman had done and smiled at him, letting Siddharth see the effect.

qa.q: How might the watchman feel when Lakshmi thanks him for holding the umbrella?
qa.a: Seen and appreciated, since he smiles back and his shoulders ease.

grounding: A child says thank you as a habit without feeling, and modelling by an adult plants the practice.
